Bahubali (IAST: Bāhubalī, lit. 'one with strong arms') was the son of Rishabhanatha (the first tirthankara of Jainism) and the brother of the chakravartin Bharata. He is a revered figure in Jainism. He is said to have meditated motionless for 12 years in a standing posture (kayotsarga), with climbing plants having grown around his legs. After his 12 years of meditation, he is said to have attained omniscience (kevala jnana).
Bahubali's other names are Kammateshwara and Gommateshwara, the namesake of the Gommateshwara statue dedicated to him.[2]
The Adipurana, a 9th-century Sanskrit poem, deals with the ten lives of the first tirthankara, Rishabhanatha and his two sons Bharata and Bahubali. It was composed by Jinasena, a Digambara monk.[3]
According to Jain texts, Bahubali was born to Rishabhanatha and Sunanda of the Ikshvaku dynasty in Ayodhya.[4][5][6][7] He studied medicine, archery, floriculture and gemology. He had a son named Somakirti, who is referred to as Mahabala.[1] In Jinasena's Adipurana, Bahubali is classified as the first of the 24 Kamadevas of the current half-cycle of time. The text describes his physical attractiveness, noting that women referred to him by epithets such as Manobhava, Manoja, Manmatha, Angaja, and Madana.[8]
Before renouncing worldly life to become a monk, Rishabhanatha distributed his kingdom among his 100 sons. Bharata received the kingdom of Vinita (Ayodhya), while Bahubali received the southern kingdom of Asmaka, with Podanapur as its capital.[9] Following his military conquests (digvijaya) across six regions, Bharata returned to Ayodhya with his army and his chakra-ratna weapon.[9] According to tradition, the weapon stopped at the city's entrance, signaling that his 99 brothers had not yet submitted to his imperial authority.[10] While 98 of his brothers surrendered their kingdoms and became Jain monks, Bahubali refused to submit.[11] Jain texts state that Bahubali possessed a superior physical constitution (vajra-rşabhanārācasamhanana) equal to Bharata's, leading him to challenge his brother's authority.[12]
The ministers on both sides gave the following argument to prevent war; "The brothers themselves, cannot be killed by any means; they are in their last incarnations in transmigration, and possess bodies which no weapon may mortally wound in warfare! Let them fight out the issue by themselves in other ways."[13] It was then decided that to settle the dispute, three kinds of contests between Bharata and Bahubali would be held. These were eye-fight (staring at each other)(drishti-yuddha), water-fight (jala-yuddha), and wrestling (malla-yuddha). Bahubali won all the three contests over his elder brother, Bharata.[9][14]
The Adipurana further narrates that, after losing the wrestling contest, Bharata became angry and used his divine weapon, the chakra-ratna, against Bahubali. But Bahubali was invincible to it, so the weapon just went around him, lost its power, and stopped near him. SOURCE namobuddy.com (The Story of Bahubali: From Battle to Liberation | Namo Buddy):
The Battle Between Brothers
Bahubali was the son of Rishabhanatha (Adinath), the first Tirthankara of the current cosmic cycle. When Rishabhanatha renounced the world to become a monk, his eldest son Bharata inherited the kingdom and declared himself Chakravarti — the emperor of all the earth.
Bharata demanded that all kings, including his brothers, submit to his sovereignty. Ninety-eight of his brothers took monkhood rather than submit. But Bahubali, the youngest and strongest, refused to bow before Bharata. A great battle seemed inevitable.
To avoid mass bloodshed, the advisors proposed three kinds of single combat: eye-battle (staring contest), water-battle (wrestling in water), and wrestling (malla-yuddha). Bahubali won all three. He had the power to imprison Bharata — but the moment of victory became the moment of illumination.
The Moment of Renunciation
Standing over the defeated Bharata, with his fist raised to strike, Bahubali had an epiphany. He thought: 'I fought for a kingdom. But what is a kingdom? A piece of earth. And I am standing on the same earth I am fighting over. I have already conquered this — why do I not conquer myself?'
In that moment, he released Bharata, uprooted his own hair — the Jain gesture of renunciation — and stood in the forest, motionless, in kayotsarga (body-abandonment meditation). He vowed not to move until he attained liberation.
A year passed. Creepers grew up around his legs. Birds nested in his hair. Insects crawled over him. He did not move. His sisters, who had become nuns, came to encourage him. They said: 'Bahubali, you have done everything right — except one thing. Surrender your ego. Get down from the elephant of pride.'
Liberation and the Gommateshwara Statue
The obstacle to Bahubali's liberation was subtle. He had renounced everything — kingdom, family, comfort — but one attachment remained: pride. He stood in the forest rather than walking through Bharata's kingdom, because he did not want to bow to his older brother even symbolically.
When his sisters helped him see this, he stepped down from his pride. In that moment, the remaining karma dissolved and he attained Kevala-jnana (omniscience) and then liberation.
To honor this extraordinary achievement, the Jain kings of Karnataka erected the world-famous Gommateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola around the 10th century CE. Standing 57 feet tall, this monolithic statue is one of the largest free-standing stone sculptures in the world and depicts Bahubali in his year-long standing meditation, with vines around his legs and an expression of perfect serenity.
